subsystems.name: Star-energy capture
subsystems.role: collects nearly all of the star's light instead of letting it escape.

subsystems.name: Computing substrate
subsystems.role: the actual active material — computing elements built at atomic scale so they are fast and cheap per operation.

subsystems.name: Nested shells
subsystems.role: each shell runs on the waste heat of the one inside it, at a lower temperature.

subsystems.name: Thermal management
subsystems.role: every bit of energy must eventually leave as infrared, so the whole structure is a giant heat engine.

subsystems.name: Structural support
subsystems.role: keeps shells from falling into the star or colliding, without needing impossible material strength.

subsystems.name: Manufacturing and repair
subsystems.role: builds and replaces shell area on a scale far larger than a planet's surface.

buildSteps.title: Harvest material
buildSteps.detail: Disassemble asteroids, moons and eventually planets to obtain rock, metal and volatiles — the raw mass of any megastructure has to come from somewhere.

buildSteps.title: Build a Dyson swarm first
buildSteps.detail: Rather than one rigid shell, launch enormous numbers of independent collectors and habitats in orbits around the star; this is stable and incrementally expandable.

buildSteps.title: Build orbital industry
buildSteps.detail: Use the collected energy to power mining, refining and fabrication that runs off the swarm itself.

buildSteps.title: Scale to planetary-area computing
buildSteps.detail: Deploy the first computing layers as flat, radiatively cooled panels — a planet's worth of data centres, then thousands of times that.

buildSteps.title: Nest successive shells
buildSteps.detail: Place cooler computing shells further out, each sized to absorb the infrared the inner shell rejects, so energy is reused several times before it escapes.

buildSteps.title: Atomically engineer the substrate
buildSteps.detail: Replace bulk machinery with computing elements built atom by atom, minimising mass and the energy lost to moving information.

buildSteps.title: Close the thermodynamics
buildSteps.detail: Tune the whole stack so the outermost shell radiates at close to the temperature of surrounding space, extracting the maximum work from each unit of stellar energy.

buildSteps.title: Run and maintain
buildSteps.detail: Self-replicating units repair and replace shell area indefinitely, since nothing physical lasts forever.

prerequisites.why: nothing remotely this large has been built or even seriously prototyped; we cannot yet build a single large space habitat at scale.
only simple automated factories exist; exponential self-replication on this scale does not.
erasing one bit costs at least kT·ln2 of energy; laboratory experiments have approached this, but real computers are roughly a billion times less efficient, and cooler operation lowers the limit.
the substrate would need mechanosynthesis — placing atoms deliberately — which remains laboratory-level research.
logic that gives back most of its energy instead of turning it into heat is a demonstrated principle but not a working technology at scale.

prerequisites.tech: Full stellar and planetary resource control
prerequisites.why: required mass and energy exceed anything a present civilisation commands by many orders of magnitude.

pathway.milestone: terrestrial and orbital data centres powered by large solar arrays
pathway.unlocks: experience in scaling and cooling computation.

pathway.milestone: space-based solar power and orbital manufacturing
pathway.unlocks: energy and materials sourced off Earth's surface.

pathway.milestone: a partial Dyson swarm: a growing cloud of collectors and radiator-panels doing computation
pathway.unlocks: energy capture far beyond any planetary budget, and the material supply to keep expanding.

pathway.milestone: multiple nested shells reusing waste heat
pathway.unlocks: computation limited mainly by thermodynamics rather than resources — assuming the physics of atomic-scale computing and self-replication can actually be realised.
